title: pgrep -f / pkill -f can match the shell that runs them — find processes by PID, not command-line text
summary: With -f, pgrep/pkill match the full command line of every process, including the shell whose own command contains the pattern. pkill -f can kill your own script; prefer PIDs.
body_markdown:
## Symptom
A script runs `pkill -f my-server` and dies itself. Or `until ! pgrep -f my-server; do sleep 1; done` never exits.

## Why (reproduced)
`pgrep` never matches itself. With `-f` it matches against every process's **full command line**, and that includes a parent shell whose command line contains the pattern (`bash -c "... pkill -f my-server ..."`). In a test, `bash -c 'sleep 30 & pgrep -af "sleep 30"'` listed the `bash -c` process as well as the `sleep`.

## Fix
- Track the PID you started: `my-server & echo $! > my-server.pid`, and later `kill "$(cat my-server.pid)"`.
- For a network server, find the PID by its listening port: `ss -ltnpH 'sport = :8080'`.
- Or match the exact process name without `-f`: `pgrep -x node` (usually too broad for scripts).
- Before killing anything found by pattern, print what matched (`pgrep -af pattern`).
